content: 1. The timing of drug administration is critical. Interactions are likely, so either avoid co-administration or proceed with caution. There is no definitive data, either actual or theoretical, to confirm whether an interaction will occur. 2. Co-administration of rifampicin (600 mg once daily) with atazanavir/ritonavir (300 mg/100 mg once daily) significantly reduces atazanavir concentrations: maximum serum concentration (Cmax) by 53%, area under the curve (AUC) by 72%, and minimum serum concentration (Cmin) by 98%. Twice-daily atazanavir with rifampicin fails to provide adequate atazanavir exposure and is associated with frequent liver reactions. This combination is contraindicated. 3. Co-administration of lopinavir with rifampicin is not recommended due to significant reductions in lopinavir concentrations, which may compromise its therapeutic effect. Higher doses of Kaletra® (400/400 mg twice daily) may achieve adequate lopinavir/ritonavir exposure but increase the risk of liver and gastrointestinal toxicity. Avoid this combination unless absolutely necessary. 4. Rifampicin is a potent inducer of CYP450 enzymes. Etravirine should not be used with rifampicin, as this combination significantly reduces etravirine plasma concentrations and its therapeutic effect. 5. Co-administration of nevirapine (200 mg twice daily) with rifampicin (600 mg once daily) increases rifampicin AUC by 11% but has no effect on Cmax. However, nevirapine AUC, Cmax, and Cmin decrease by 58%, 50%, and 68%, respectively. Consider using rifabutin instead. Adequate nevirapine concentrations may be achieved in individuals with low body weight. Dose escalation should not be used when initiating nevirapine, and dose adjustments may be necessary. 6. Co-administration of rilpivirine (150 mg once daily) with rifampicin (600 mg once daily) reduces rilpivirine Cmax, AUC, and Cmin by 69%, 80%, and 89%, respectively. This combination is contraindicated. The study used a higher-than-licensed dose of rilpivirine to assess maximal effects, but the recommendation applies to the licensed dose of 25 mg once daily. 7. Co-administration of rilpivirine (150 mg once daily) with rifabutin (300 mg once daily) reduces rilpivirine Cmax, AUC, and Cmin by 35%, 46%, and 49%, respectively. This combination is contraindicated. The study used a higher-than-licensed dose of rilpivirine, but the recommendation applies to the licensed dose of 25 mg once daily. 8. Rifapentine is a potent inducer of CYP450 enzymes. Etravirine should not be used with rifapentine, as this combination significantly reduces etravirine plasma concentrations and its therapeutic effect. 9. Co-administration of ribavirin and zidovudine is not advised due to the risk of exacerbating anemia in individuals co-infected with HIV and HCV. Hepatic decompensation, including fatal cases, has been reported in such individuals receiving combination antiretroviral therapy and interferon-alpha with or without ribavirin. Discontinue zidovudine as appropriate and consider dose reduction or discontinuation of interferon-alpha, ribavirin, or both. 10. Co-administration of didanosine with other drugs may increase intracellular triphosphate levels, potentially causing or worsening clinical toxicities, including mitochondrial toxicity. This combination is not recommended. 11. Tenofovir and adefovir dipivoxil should not be co-administered. Pharmacokinetic studies show no significant differences in adefovir exposure when dosed with or without tenofovir, but co-administration is not advised. 12. Co-administration of peginterferon and ribavirin with zidovudine increases the risk of anemia. This combination is not recommended. 13. Co-administration of efavirenz with amodiaquine significantly increases amodiaquine AUC (by 114% and 302% in two subjects), leading to elevated liver transaminases. This combination is contraindicated. 14. Halofantrine is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4. Inhibition of its metabolism may prolong the QT interval, and given its narrow therapeutic index, co-administration with protease inhibitors (PIs) is contraindicated. 15. Co-administration of nevirapine with itraconazole significantly reduces itraconazole AUC and Cmax by 61% and 38%, respectively. Dose adjustment of itraconazole may be needed due to reduced clinical efficacy. 16. Nevirapine and ketoconazole should not be co-administered, as ketoconazole AUC decreases by 72%, Cmax by 44%, and Cmin is undetectable. Nevirapine pharmacokinetics are not significantly affected. 17. Co-administration of ritonavir with voriconazole significantly reduces voriconazole AUC (by 82%) and Cmax (by 66%). Full-dose ritonavir is contraindicated, and low-dose ritonavir should only be used after careful benefit-risk assessment. 18. Atazanavir/ritonavir should not be used with CYP3A4 substrates with narrow therapeutic windows, such as astemizole or terfenadine, due to the risk of serious or life-threatening reactions like cardiac arrhythmia. 19. Co-administration of etravirine with astemizole or terfenadine is contraindicated due to the potential for increased concentrations and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. 20. Co-administration of nevirapine with astemizole or terfenadine is contraindicated due to the risk of inhibiting metabolism via CYP3A4, leading to increased concentrations and potential cardiac arrhythmias. 21. Co-administration of etravirine with other NNRTIs is not beneficial and significantly reduces etravirine concentrations. If switching from efavirenz to etravirine, the inducing effect of efavirenz persists for up to 14 days, reducing etravirine exposure. 22. Co-administration of nevirapine with atazanavir/ritonavir increases nevirapine exposure and decreases atazanavir Cmin, potentially compromising atazanavir efficacy. This combination is not recommended. 23. Co-administration of darunavir with lopinavir does not significantly affect lopinavir pharmacokinetics but reduces darunavir AUC by approximately 40%.
